title: Query Operators
summary: Build precise filters with comparison, logical, element, array and regular-expression operators, and learn how MongoDB combines conditions.
introduction: Equality filters only get you so far. Real questions sound like "peripherals under 100 that are in stock" or "products missing a rating", and MongoDB answers them with query operators: keywords beginning with `$` that you nest inside the filter document. This lesson covers the operator families you will use daily, shows how conditions combine, and points out the two mistakes that silently return the wrong documents. It uses the six products inserted in the previous lesson.
learningObjectives: Combine conditions with implicit AND, $and, $or and $not
Test for missing fields and types with $exists and $type
Match arrays and patterns with $all, $size, $elemMatch and regular expressions

blocks.text: A filter is itself a document. A plain field–value pair means *equals*; an operator document in place of the value means *compare like this*. Several fields in one filter are combined with AND. Everything in this lesson follows from those three rules, so keep them in mind as the examples get longer. If you did not run the previous lesson, re-create the collection first:

blocks.code:
use shop
db.products.drop()
db.products.insertMany([
  { _id: 1, name: 'Mechanical keyboard', price: 89.5, category: 'peripherals', stock: 12, tags: ['usb', 'backlit'], rating: 4.6 },
  { _id: 2, name: 'Wireless mouse', price: 24.99, category: 'peripherals', stock: 0, tags: ['wireless', 'usb'], rating: 4.1 },
  { _id: 3, name: '27-inch monitor', price: 219, category: 'displays', stock: 5, tags: ['4k', 'hdmi'], rating: 4.8 },
  { _id: 4, name: 'Desk lamp', price: 24.5, category: 'office', stock: 40, tags: ['led'] },
  { _id: 5, name: 'USB-C hub', price: 39, category: 'peripherals', stock: 8, tags: ['usb'], rating: 3.9 },
  { _id: 6, name: 'Webcam', price: 59, category: 'peripherals', stock: 3, tags: ['usb', 'video'], rating: 4.3, discontinued: true }
])

rows: equal to the value (same as writing the value directly)
not equal to the value, or missing
greater than, greater than or equal
less than, less than or equal
none of the listed values, or missing

blocks.text: Two operators on the same field go into one operator document, which reads as a range. `$in` replaces a chain of equality checks and also matches when the field is an array containing one of the values:

blocks.code:
db.products.find({ price: { $gte: 30, $lt: 100 } }, { _id: 0, name: 1, price: 1 })
db.products.find({ category: { $in: ['displays', 'office'] } }, { _id: 0, name: 1, category: 1 })

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Writing the same field twice, as in `{ price: { $gt: 30 }, price: { $lt: 100 } }`, does not give you a range. The filter is a JavaScript object, and the second `price` key silently replaces the first, so the query only checks `$lt: 100`. Put both operators in one document, `{ price: { $gt: 30, $lt: 100 } }`, or use `$and` when the conditions are on the same field but cannot be merged.

Separate fields in a filter are already ANDed, so `$and` is only needed when you must repeat a field or combine several `$or` clauses. `$or` takes an array of filters and matches when any of them does; `$nor` matches when none does; `$not` wraps an operator document and negates it, matching missing fields too.

blocks.code:
db.products.find({ category: 'peripherals', stock: { $gt: 0 } }, { _id: 0, name: 1, stock: 1 })
db.products.find({ $or: [{ stock: 0 }, { discontinued: true }] }, { _id: 0, name: 1 })

blocks.text: The first query reads "peripherals AND stock greater than zero". The second reads "out of stock OR discontinued", the kind of filter a shop uses to hide products from a listing. An `$or` whose clauses are all on the same field is better written with `$in`.

Because documents in a collection may differ, you sometimes need to ask about the field itself rather than its value. `$exists: false` finds documents that lack a field, and `$type` checks the BSON type by name. Remember from the [Documents and Collections](/tutorials/mongodb/documents-collections) lesson that mongosh stores whole numbers as `int` and fractions as `double`:

blocks.code:
db.products.find({ rating: { $exists: false } }, { _id: 0, name: 1 })
db.products.find({ price: { $type: 'int' } }, { _id: 0, name: 1, price: 1 })

blocks.text: Use `$type: 'number'` to match any numeric type at once. A field set to `null` *exists*, so `{ rating: null }` matches both documents where `rating` is `null` and documents where it is missing, while `{ rating: { $exists: false } }` matches only the latter.

A plain value against an array field matches when any element equals it, so `{ tags: 'usb' }` finds every USB product. The array operators ask more specific questions: `$all` requires every listed value to be present, `$size` matches an exact length, and `$elemMatch` requires one single element to satisfy several conditions at once, which matters for arrays of documents such as order lines.

blocks.code:
db.products.find({ tags: { $all: ['usb', 'backlit'] } }, { _id: 0, name: 1 })
db.products.find({ tags: { $size: 1 } }, { _id: 0, name: 1, tags: 1 })

blocks.text: The difference shows with arrays of documents. Two dotted conditions, `{ 'lines.sku': 'K1', 'lines.qty': { $gte: 2 } }`, match an order where *one* line has `sku: 'K1'` and a *different* line has a quantity of 2 or more. `{ lines: { $elemMatch: { sku: 'K1', qty: { $gte: 2 } } } }` keeps both conditions on the same element, which is almost always what you mean.

A JavaScript regular expression in place of a value matches strings by pattern; `$regex` with a string pattern does the same from languages without regex literals. The `i` flag makes the match case-insensitive. Only patterns anchored at the start, such as `/^w/`, can use an index; a pattern like `/cam/` scans every document, so keep it for small collections or use Atlas Search for real text search.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Find the peripherals that are either rated 4.5 or higher or cost less than 30, excluding discontinued ones. You will need `$or` inside an implicit AND. Then rewrite `{ $or: [{ category: 'displays' }, { category: 'office' }] }` with `$in` and check that both return the same two products.

questions.question: Which filter finds products priced between 20 and 50 inclusive?
questions.explanation: Both bounds go into one operator document on the same field. Repeating the `price` key would discard the first condition.

questions.question: The filter `{ tags: 'usb' }` matches a document whose `tags` array contains `'usb'` among other values.
questions.explanation: A scalar value against an array field matches when any element equals that value. To require several values at once, use `$all`.
